strengths: Addresses a genuinely challenging and underexplored problem: sparse-view (three-camera) reconstruction of dynamic, emissive, semi-transparent fire, which is not well handled by existing dynamic 3DGS methods.

The pipeline design is well-motivated: decoupling static background (via stereo+monocular depth fusion) from dynamic fire (via flow-initialized FreeTimeGS) is a sensible strategy for the under-constrained sparse-view setting, and each design choice is ablated (Tab. 2 and per-scene tables).

Novel and practical hardware contribution: a custom LED/microcontroller-based rolling-shutter exploiting synchronization scheme enabling microsecond-level sub-frame alignment with unsynchronized consumer cameras — a nice systems-level contribution with potential reuse value beyond this paper.

New real-world dataset of 17 diverse fire sequences (multiple fuels, wind/backgrounds) captured with a 3-camera 400Hz rig, with per-scene quantitative breakdowns provided in supplementary — useful benchmark for future fire/volumetric dynamic reconstruction work.

Quantitative results show clear improvements in flame-region metrics (PSNRflame, SSIMflame) and depth plausibility (RMSEdepth) over two 4DGS baselines, and qualitative figures (Fig. 9) visibly show baselines producing degenerate depth/geometry while the proposed method preserves plausible geometry.

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of rolling-shutter modeling, synchronization, flow-based initialization, and static/dynamic separation, including full per-scene numbers in the supplementary.
weaknesses: No ground-truth 3D/4D geometry is available for quantitative evaluation of fire dynamics; the primary geometric metric (RMSEdepth) is only a comparison against a monocular depth estimator after linear alignment, which is itself an approximate, potentially biased pseudo-ground-truth — this weakens the strength of the central quantitative claims about geometric plausibility.

The two baselines (4DGS Wu et al. and 4DGS Yang et al.) are used with parameters tuned for the DyNeRF flame_salmon scene and are known to require dense multi-view input; comparing them under-optimized/out-of-domain against a method specifically engineered for this sparse 3-view/fire setting risks an unfair or at least not fully illuminating comparison — additional baselines more suited to sparse-view or volumetric/emissive phenomena (e.g., physics-informed smoke/fire reconstruction methods, or sparse-view NeRF/3DGS variants) would strengthen the evidence.

The linear velocity + Gaussian lifetime model is a fairly coarse motion representation for highly turbulent flame dynamics; the paper itself acknowledges this in the limitations, but no analysis (e.g., of failure cases, temporal blur, or motion error) is given to quantify how much this approximation costs in practice.

Ablations (Table 2) show several proposed components (rolling shutter modeling, sub-frame sync) yield very small or statistically ambiguous quantitative gains (e.g., GlobalShutter vs Baseline differences are within noise), which somewhat undercuts the significance of the rolling-shutter/synchronization contribution as presented, despite its engineering novelty.

The dataset, while a nice contribution, is relatively small in scale (17 fifteen-second sequences, 100-frame subsequences) and captured in similar outdoor fire-pit-like conditions; generalization to other flame contexts (indoor fires, wildfires, different scales) is untested.

Clarity issues: the manuscript conflates FireGS/Gaussians on Fire naming, and some methodological details (e.g., how segmentation between static/dynamic regions is obtained beyond the minimum-intensity projection, exact voxel grid resolution, or computational cost breakdown for preprocessing steps like optical flow and stereo) are under-specified for full reproducibility.

No user study or perceptual evaluation is included despite emphasizing 'photo-realistic' qualitative results; reliance on LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM for emissive, high-frequency content may not fully capture perceptual quality differences highlighted in the qualitative figures.

strengths: Tackles a genuinely under-explored and challenging problem (photorealistic reconstruction of real fire from only three sparse views), which has clear applied value for VFX, simulation validation, and safety/monitoring applications.

The overall pipeline is sensibly engineered: decoupling static background (stereo+monocular depth fusion) from dynamic fire (flow-initialized FreeTimeGS) is a reasonable strategy to cope with severely under-constrained sparse-view geometry.

The custom LED/rolling-shutter based hardware synchronization scheme for achieving microsecond-level sub-frame alignment on unsynchronized consumer cameras is a nice practical engineering contribution that could be useful beyond this specific application.
A new real-world multi-view fire dataset (17 sequences, diverse fuels/backgrounds, 400 Hz capture) is provided and could be a valuable community resource if fully released.
Ablations (NoSync, RandFlow, JointOpt, GlobalShutter) are included and mostly support the intuitive design choices (flow initialization, static/dynamic separation, synchronization).
weaknesses: The technical contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing off-the-shelf components (COLMAP, PatchMatchStereo, DepthAnythingV2, MEMFOF, FreeTimeGS) rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical advance; the paper does not clearly isolate what is conceptually novel beyond integration.

The comparison against 4DGS (Wu et al.) and 4DGS (Yang et al.) is not well controlled: both baselines are randomly initialized and trained with author-provided hyperparameters tuned for the DyNeRF flame-salmon scene, while the proposed method benefits from privileged dense stereo/monocular depth initialization and flow-based initialization not available to the baselines. This makes the reported gains difficult to attribute to a specific methodological advance rather than to unequal initialization/regularization budgets. A fairer comparison (e.g., providing baselines with the same depth/flow priors, or comparing against vanilla FreeTimeGS without flow init) is missing.

The RMSE-depth metric is computed against a monocular depth *prediction* (DepthAnythingV2) rather than any ground-truth geometry, and the static-scene branch of the proposed method is itself regularized using the same monocular depth prior during training — this risks a partially circular evaluation that mechanically favors the proposed pipeline.

The GlobalShutter ablation shows essentially no measurable difference from the full rolling-shutter model (e.g., PSNR_flame 27.46 vs 27.48), undermining the claimed importance of the rolling-shutter modeling contribution highlighted heavily in Sec. 3.3, despite the amount of methodological space devoted to it.

No quantitative comparison is provided against any prior fire/smoke-specific reconstruction method (e.g., physics-informed neural fields, tomographic approaches), despite these being discussed at length in related work; the only baselines are generic dynamic 3DGS methods not designed for emissive/transparent phenomena, which weakens claims of state-of-the-art performance on the specific fire task.

Reproducibility is limited: full dataset and code are stated as "to be released," with only a single example scene included in supplementary material, making independent verification of the dataset and results currently impossible.

The explicit linear-velocity, single-lifetime Gaussian model is acknowledged to poorly capture turbulent, non-linear flame motion, and no quantitative frequency-domain analysis is given to substantiate the "high-frequency reconstruction" framing used in the title and abstract.

Minor clarity/consistency issues: inconsistent citation numbering for Wu et al. 4DGS (appears as both [91] and [92]), and some informal phrasing (e.g., "archives higher" instead of "achieves higher").

strengths: Tackles a genuinely difficult and underexplored problem (dynamic fire reconstruction from very sparse, only 3 views) with a well-motivated, complete pipeline that combines several practical engineering contributions: static/dynamic scene decomposition via minimum-intensity projection, stereo+monocular depth fusion for the background, and a flow-initialized FreeTimeGS-based dynamic Gaussian representation for the flame.

The custom LED-based hardware synchronization scheme that exploits rolling-shutter readout for microsecond-level sub-frame alignment across unsynchronized commodity cameras is a creative, low-cost solution to a real practical bottleneck in multi-view high-speed capture, and is clearly explained with supporting derivations (Eq. 9) and empirical characterization (readout time, achieved precision).

The authors contribute a new real-world multi-view fire dataset (17 sequences, diverse fuels: propane, wood, cardboard, paper, with varying wind/intensity conditions), which is valuable to the community as a benchmark for this niche but important application area (also relevant to related works such as wildfire simulation cited in the paper).

Thorough ablation study (Table 2, with full per-scene breakdowns in supplementary) isolates the contribution of rolling-shutter modeling, synchronization, flow-based initialization, and static/dynamic separation, providing good evidence that each pipeline component matters, especially flow initialization and static/dynamic decoupling.

Quantitative results show clear advantages in flame-region metrics (PSNR_flame, SSIM_flame) and especially depth consistency (RMSE_depth) over the two 4DGS baselines, and qualitative comparisons (Fig. 9) visually support the claim that competing methods produce spatially degenerate reconstructions under sparse-view conditions.

The paper is well-written, with clear methodology, informative figures illustrating intermediate representations (Fig. 4, 5), and a discussion of limitations that is specific and tied to the method's actual assumptions (linear velocity, background-foreground independence) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are limited to two general-purpose 4DGS variants (Wu et al., Yang et al.), neither designed for extremely sparse (3-view) capture nor for emissive/transparent phenomena; the paper does not compare against the FreeTimeGS baseline it builds on, nor against other recent dynamic Gaussian methods (e.g., MoSca, Dynamic 3D Gaussians, DynMF) or physics-informed fire/smoke reconstruction methods, making it harder to judge how much of the improvement stems from the proposed flow-initialization/decomposition versus simply using a representation (FreeTimeGS) better suited to non-rigid motion.

Quantitative depth evaluation relies on RMSE against an aligned monocular depth estimate rather than true depth ground truth, which is a fairly weak and potentially circular proxy for 3D geometric accuracy given that monocular depth is also used elsewhere in the pipeline for regularization/initialization.

The rolling-shutter ablation (GlobalShutter) shows negligible quantitative benefit despite being presented as a core contribution (#4 in the intro contributions list and a dedicated methodology section), somewhat undercutting its claimed significance; the manuscript acknowledges this but does not fully reconcile the emphasis placed on it with the empirical results.

The linear-velocity, single-lifetime Gaussian motion model is a strong simplification of turbulent flame dynamics, and the paper's own qualitative results/limitations section suggest this leads to temporal blurring; no experiments directly probe how well the method captures higher-frequency turbulent structures beyond global visual plausibility.

Full-frame metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are sometimes lower than the 4DGS (Yang et al.) baseline, and while the authors offer a plausible explanation (joint background/foreground adaptation vs. their fixed static background), this raises the question of whether the static-background assumption is a genuine limitation in scenes with more background-fire interaction (e.g., heat shimmer, smoke-tinted lighting) not thoroughly analyzed.

Reproducibility depends on future release of code/full dataset (only a single example scene included in supplementary); given the highly custom multi-camera hardware/synchronization setup, exact replication by other groups without the same rig may be difficult regardless of code availability.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and challenging problem (sparse-view 3D reconstruction of fire), which existing GS methods are convincingly shown to fail at via multiple baselines (4DGS variants, Grid4D, FreeTimeGS) and multiple failure-mode analyses (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift).

Provides a full, reasonably well-engineered pipeline: stereo+monocular depth fusion for the static background, optical-flow-based 3D voxel flow initialization for transient Gaussians with explicit lifetime/velocity parameters, and a masked alpha loss to prevent dynamic Gaussians leaking into the static scene.

Practical systems contribution: an inexpensive ESP32-based rolling-shutter LED synchronization scheme achieving ~15 µs sub-frame precision on unsynchronized consumer GoPro cameras, which is a nice piece of applied engineering with clear technical justification (readout time/row-time analysis).

New real-world (17 sequences, various fuels) and synthetic (Mantaflow + Blender, ray-traced, with ground-truth 640^3 velocity fields) datasets are introduced and will reportedly be released, which is valuable for future work on this understudied problem.

Introduces a new density-weighted volumetric velocity evaluation protocol (DVE) tailored to transient, non-persistent primitives, addressing a real gap since standard trajectory- or 2D-flow-based dynamic GS metrics do not apply to fire.

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparisons (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/RMSE-depth, masked flame-region metrics), video-level perceptual metric (CGVQM), synthetic velocity-field metrics, thorough ablations (sync offset, flow init, joint vs. separate optimization, alpha loss), and per-scene breakdowns in supplementary material.

Clear qualitative evidence (streamplots, depth maps, temporal sequences) supporting the quantitative claims, and discussion of a genuine trade-off between visual fidelity and physical plausibility of motion (JointOpt/NoMask ablations).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is primarily a combination and adaptation of existing components (3DGS, FreeTimeGS-style velocity/lifetime Gaussians, PatchMatchStereo, DepthAnythingV2, MEMFOF optical flow) rather than a fundamentally new representation or algorithm; the main innovations are the flow-to-3D fusion for initialization and the masked decomposition strategy.

The linear constant-velocity motion model is explicitly acknowledged as unable to capture turbulent, non-linear flame dynamics, which is a core physical property of fire; this could limit fidelity for larger or more chaotic flames beyond what is shown.

Quantitative dynamics evaluation (DVE) relies on only 3 synthetic scenes (150 total velocity fields from just 3 simulations), which is a fairly small and possibly non-diverse basis for validating a new metric and drawing strong conclusions about motion-reconstruction superiority.

Comparisons are restricted to GS-based baselines; while the compute-cost justification for excluding physics-informed/tomographic fire-specific methods is reasonable, it leaves open how the proposed approach compares against methods specifically designed for this domain (e.g., PINF, tomographic reconstruction), which would help contextualize the significance of the improvement.

The practical setup (three calibrated/synchronized cameras with custom hardware, static frame acquisition or min-intensity background extraction) adds real-world deployment complexity and may not trivially generalize to more complex environments (e.g., moving background elements, smoke-heavy or occluded scenes), a limitation partially acknowledged but not empirically stress-tested.

The introduction and framing use somewhat strong/promotional language (e.g., 'fundamentally fail,' 'solve this,' 'no existing method... reliably reconstruct') that slightly overstates the generality of the claims relative to the fairly constrained experimental conditions (controlled outdoor fires, fixed 3-camera rigs).

strengths: Tackles a genuinely underexplored and difficult problem: sparse-view (3-camera) reconstruction of highly dynamic, emissive, semi-transparent fire, which is shown to break existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods (4DGS variants, Grid4D, FreeTimeGS) in clear and reproducible ways (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift).

The decoupled static/dynamic pipeline (dense stereo + monocular depth fusion for background, flow-projected 3D voxel field for flame initialization) is a sensible and well-motivated engineering solution to the severe under-constrained geometry problem posed by only three views.

The custom ESP32-based visual synchronization scheme exploiting rolling-shutter timing to achieve microsecond-level sub-frame alignment on commodity GoPro cameras is a creative, low-cost, and practically useful contribution for high-speed multi-view capture beyond just this application.

A new density-weighted volumetric evaluation protocol (DVE) is proposed to assess 3D motion-field accuracy against simulated ground-truth velocity fields, addressing a real gap since standard 2D image metrics cannot capture the physical plausibility of reconstructed dynamics.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: quantitative comparisons across multiple visual and depth metrics, a video-level perceptual metric (CGVQM), and informative ablations (NoSync, RandFlow, JointOpt, NoMask) that reveal a meaningful trade-off between visual fidelity and physically accurate motion.

A sizeable real-world dataset (17 sequences, multiple fuel types, 400Hz capture) and synthetic Mantaflow/Blender fire scenes with ground-truth velocity fields are introduced and promised for release, which could be a useful resource for future work on transient/volumetric phenomena.
weaknesses: The core dynamic representation (per-Gaussian lifetime, linear velocity, temporal opacity modulation) is explicitly adopted from FreeTimeGS, and the 3DGS backbone for statics is vanilla; the genuinely new elements are largely limited to the flow-based 3D initialization and the alpha/mask loss, making the algorithmic novelty comparatively incremental relative to the paper's framing as solving a fundamentally new representational problem.

Baseline comparison may be less than fair: competing methods are initialized from COLMAP points (which struggle badly on flame regions by the authors' own admission) or a RoMa-based scheme shown to fail on fire, while the proposed method benefits from a bespoke flow-based initialization tailored specifically to this content; baseline hyperparameters were also taken from an unrelated DyNeRF scene rather than tuned for this dataset, which could inflate the apparent performance gap.

The physical-plausibility validation (DVE metric) rests on only 3 synthetic base scenes (despite 150 generated velocity fields, these derive from a small set of underlying simulations), limiting the statistical strength of claims about superior motion-field recovery.

The constant-velocity, single-lifetime Gaussian motion model is acknowledged to be a poor fit for turbulent, non-linear flame dynamics, and the static/dynamic decomposition assumes minimal foreground-background interaction, which the authors admit breaks down for smoke-rich or larger-scale fires — this meaningfully limits generality beyond the curated, mostly small-to-medium controlled-burn scenes shown.

Strong claims (e.g., that fire reconstruction is a fundamental failure case for all existing GS methods, or that fire representation requires a wholesale rethinking of Gaussian Splatting) are somewhat overstated given the comparison is limited to four GS baselines under a single dataset regime and no comparison to specialized (non-GS) fire/smoke reconstruction methods is quantitatively attempted.

The custom synchronization hardware, while clever, depends on careful per-camera characterization of rolling-shutter timing and specific hardware; its claimed reproducibility with "affordable commodity hardware" may be optimistic given the calibration effort required, somewhat limiting practical accessibility despite the low component cost.

The paper combines several distinct contributions (representation, hardware, dataset, evaluation protocol) that are each treated somewhat briefly rather than being individually developed and stress-tested in depth, giving an impression of breadth over depth in the core technical contribution.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously demonstrates a genuine failure mode of existing dynamic 3DGS methods (4DGS variants, Grid4D, FreeTimeGS) when applied to sparse-view fire reconstruction, providing clear motivation for the work.

The core technical idea of decoupling static background (dense stereo + monocular depth fusion) from transient flame Gaussians (flow-initialized, with explicit lifetime/velocity parameters) is well-reasoned and specifically tailored to the failure modes identified.

Introduces a practical, low-cost LED/rolling-shutter-based sub-frame synchronization scheme for consumer cameras, which is a nice systems-level contribution enabling high-frequency (400Hz) multi-view capture without specialized hardware.

Proposes a new evaluation protocol (density-weighted volumetric evaluation, DVE) using synthetic ground-truth velocity fields to assess 3D motion fidelity, addressing a real gap since standard 2D image metrics cannot capture dynamic/volumetric reconstruction quality.

Comprehensive experimental validation: 17 real fire sequences across diverse fuels/backgrounds, 3 synthetic Mantaflow/Blender scenes with dense ground-truth velocity fields, extensive ablations (NoSync, RandFlow, JointOpt, NoMask), and additional video-level perceptual metrics (CGVQM) in the supplement.
Thorough supplementary material with implementation details, per-scene breakdowns, rolling-shutter modeling, and dataset descriptions that support reproducibility.

Consistent, sizeable quantitative and qualitative improvements over all four GS baselines on both real and synthetic data, with plausible failure-mode analysis (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift) tied directly to the proposed fixes.
weaknesses: The introduction contains somewhat overstated/rhetorical claims (e.g., methods 'fundamentally fail,' fire 'violates this assumption entirely') that could be toned down to better match the more measured empirical findings later.

FreeTimeGS is compared via an unofficial third-party reimplementation with a different (RoMa-based) initialization strategy; while the paper flags this, it makes the comparison somewhat less controlled than the other baselines initialized from COLMAP.

Baselines are trained using author-provided hyperparameters tuned for the DyNeRF flame-salmon scene rather than being tuned/adapted for this specific sparse-view fire capture setting, which could understate baseline performance.
The synthetic velocity-field evaluation (DVE) is based on only 3 scenes, which is a fairly small basis for validating a newly proposed metric and drawing strong conclusions about motion fidelity.

The constant-velocity/linear motion model is acknowledged as unable to capture turbulent flame dynamics, and the static/dynamic decomposition assumes minimal background-foreground interaction (problematic for smoke-heavy or strongly interacting scenes) — these are real, non-trivial limitations for generalizing beyond the tested conditions.

No quantitative depth ground truth exists for the real-world dataset; RMSE_depth is computed against a monocular depth predictor rather than true geometry, making that metric somewhat circular/soft as validation.

Limited comparison/discussion against non-GS specialized fire/smoke reconstruction methods (tomographic, physics-informed neural fields) is justified mainly by efficiency arguments rather than empirical evidence, leaving open how the method compares in reconstruction quality to this closer prior art.
